screens.title: Introducing Behavioral Patterns: The Strategy Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why behavioral patterns matter and how the Strategy pattern helps you decouple algorithms from the clients that use them. Behavioral patterns focus on how objects interact and share responsibilities, which makes systems easier to change and test. The Strategy pattern is a classic example: it defines a common interface for related algorithms, implements each algorithm in a separate class, and lets the client pick or swap the algorithm at runtime. You will see a concrete C# example that models shipping cost calculations, and then a refactoring exercise that replaces a large switch statement with strategy classes. We will also examine common mistakes, such as coupling a context to concrete strategy creation, and practical guidance like when Strategy is overkill. By the end you should be able to choose, implement, and safely apply Strategy in small systems like discount calculators or larger subsystems like authentication. Consider where you have conditional logic tied to behavior; that is often where Strategy can reduce friction and increase testability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Introducing the Strategy Pattern
Introducing Behavioral Patterns: The Strategy Pattern
Encapsulate algorithms behind an interface so clients can choose behavior at runtime.
This lesson shows you how Strategy removes conditional branches, improves testability, and supports dependency injection in C#. Expect code examples for shipping cost and a refactoring lab for discounts.
In this lesson
Find a clear definition, real C# examples, a hands-on refactor, and practical guidance that helps you decide when to apply Strategy.
Explore Key Topics
Interchangeable Algorithms
How to define a shared interface and swap implementations at runtime.
C# Implementation
Interfaces, constructors, and a pattern-friendly context design using DI.
When Not to Use
Recognize over-engineering and when simple conditionals are fine.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Concept Snapshot
Strategy: define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each, and make them interchangeable so clients are independent of algorithm details.
Shipping Example
Discount Refactor
Why this matters
Decoupling behavior reduces change-risk, enables automated tests for individual strategies, and makes your code base easier to extend without touching existing logic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and apply the Strategy pattern in real C# code. First, you will name the core purpose of behavioral patterns and explain how they distribute responsibility between objects. Second, you will recognize the problem Strategy solves — interchangeable algorithms — and contrast it with simpler conditionals. Third, you will implement Strategy in C# by defining an interface, creating concrete strategy classes, and injecting them into a context. Finally, you will spot scenarios where Strategy improves flexibility, such as shipping calculations, discount rules, validation, or export formats, and avoid common pitfalls like over-engineering or letting the context instantiate its strategies. Each objective maps to hands-on practice: reading code, writing small strategy implementations, and refactoring a switch-based discount calculator into a Strategy-based design. As you work, test each strategy independently so you build confidence and ensure design decisions reduce complexity rather than add it.

screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide emphasizes hands-on practice and common pitfalls to avoid. You will implement a Strategy-based design in C#, writing an interface and multiple concrete strategies, then inject them into a context class. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Practice & Pitfalls
Practice and Pitfalls
What to practice and what to avoid when applying Strategy.
Practice
Write an interface, implement each strategy, inject into a context, and write tests that validate each algorithm independently.
Pitfall
Avoid letting a context decide which concrete strategy to create based on strings or flags; that couples the context and defeats the pattern’s purpose.
Use dependency injection or factories to provide strategies. If strategies share behavior, consider factoring common code into a base class or using Template Method instead. These choices keep your code maintainable and testable as requirements change.
Quick Tip
If adding a strategy means only adding a branch in a switch and nothing else, Strategy may be overkill until the behavior grows in complexity.
Check Your Understanding
Can you explain how dependency injection supports Strategy and how tests for each strategy improve confidence when changing algorithms?

screens.title: What is the Strategy Pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one in a separate class, and makes them interchangeable through a common interface. In plain terms, you move algorithm-specific code out of a client and into strategy classes that the client calls through an interface. A concrete example is shipping cost calculation: USPS, FedEx, and UPS each use distinct formulas. Instead of a large conditional inside ShippingCalculator, you create an IShippingStrategy interface and concrete strategies for each carrier. The context holds a reference to IShippingStrategy and delegates cost calculation to it. This removes conditional logic from the context and obeys the Open/Closed Principle — you can add a new carrier by adding a class rather than editing existing code. A common misconception is thinking Strategy always reduces complexity; if you have only a single simple algorithm that will not change, Strategy can be unnecessary boilerplate. The real benefit appears when algorithms vary, evolve, or must be tested independently. Try naming the responsibilities: the Strategy implements the algorithm, the Context delegates and remains ignorant of concrete types, and the Client composes them. How would you test one strategy in isolation? That question guides how you structure constructors and dependencies.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Encapsulate related algorithms behind a common interface so clients can use any of them without knowing details.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is Strategy?
Pattern Definition
Strategy encapsulates algorithms and exposes a common interface so clients can vary behavior at runtime.
• Strategy: interface that declares the algorithm signature.
• Concrete Strategy: a class that implements the interface with a specific algorithm.
• Context: holds a reference to the strategy and delegates work to it.
Analogy
Think of a media player: the player (context) uses different codecs (strategies) to decode audio or video. The player doesn’t know codec internals; it relies on the codec interface.
Concrete example — shipping strategies
// Interface
public interface IShippingStrategy
{
  double CalculateCost(Order order);
}

// Concrete strategy example
public class USPSStrategy : IShippingStrategy
{
  public double CalculateCost(Order order)
  {
    return 5.00 + (order.WeightInKg * 1.50);
  }
}
Example
USPS strategy computes a base fee plus a weight rate.
Misconception
Strategy is not always better; small static logic may not need it.
Key Takeaway

Use Strategy when you need to vary algorithms independently and test them in isolation.

screens.title: Context, Strategy, and Concrete Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the roles in Strategy clarifies responsibilities and tests. The three key roles are Strategy, Concrete Strategy, and Context. The Strategy is an interface that declares the operation signature your algorithms share. Each Concrete Strategy implements that interface with a specific algorithm. The Context holds a reference to the Strategy interface and delegates the operation to the current strategy. In C#, you typically inject the strategy via the constructor or a setter so the context remains unaware of concrete types. For example, a ShippingService takes an IShippingStrategy in its constructor and calls CalculateCost on it. That service may expose a SetStrategy method to swap strategies at runtime. Tests should exercise each concrete strategy directly, asserting algorithmic results for representative orders. A common mistake is letting the context both decide and instantiate strategies; that couples the context to strategy implementations and prevents easy testing. If strategies share common helper code, factor it into a base class or shared utility instead of embedding it in each strategy. Now imagine adding tax calculations or promotional adjustments: those concerns might be separate strategies or combined carefully, depending on cohesion.

keyIdea.title: Roles
keyIdea.text: Strategy declares behavior, Concrete Strategies implement it, and Context delegates to whichever strategy it holds.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Context & Roles
Architecture Overview
Identify how each role contributes to decoupling and testability.
Strategy
An interface declaring the operation signature like CalculateCost.
Concrete Strategy
A class implementing the algorithm for a specific case, e.g., FedEx.
Context
Holds IShippingStrategy and delegates calculation to it. Accepts strategies via DI or setter.
Design tip: keep the context lean. It should not know strategy internals or be responsible for creating concrete strategies. Prefer factories or the IoC container for that responsibility so the context stays focused on orchestration and remains easily testable.
Example — ShippingService
public class ShippingService
{
  private IShippingStrategy _shippingStrategy;

  public ShippingService(IShippingStrategy strategy)
  {
    _shippingStrategy = strategy ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(strategy));
  }

  public void SetStrategy(IShippingStrategy strategy)
  {
    _shippingStrategy = strategy ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(strategy));
  }

  public double GetShippingCost(Order order)
  {
    return _shippingStrategy.CalculateCost(order);
  }
}
Note
Using constructor injection makes the dependency explicit and simplifies unit testing.

screens.title: Implementing Strategy in C# — Interfaces and Samples
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look closely at the C# building blocks for Strategy. You need three things: an interface that declares the algorithm, at least one concrete strategy that implements the interface, and a context that holds a reference to the interface. In C#, the interface might be IShippingStrategy with a CalculateCost method that accepts an Order. Each concrete strategy implements that method with carrier-specific logic. The sample code demonstrates USPS with a base rate plus weight, FedEx using volume, and UPS using a higher base rate plus a weight multiplier. Writing small, focused strategy classes helps you test each algorithm with representative orders. A practical test creates an Order with known values and asserts the returned cost. If different strategies share code, extract helpers into a utility or a base abstract class. Remember to guard against null strategies in the context by throwing an ArgumentNullException or by providing a default strategy to keep behavior explicit and safe. Try creating a fake order in a unit test and asserting the expected costs for each concrete strategy. Implementing Strategy in C# — Interfaces and Samples means declare an interface, implement each strategy, inject into the context, and test strategies independently with representative inputs.. In practical terms, define ishippingstrategy and concrete implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › C# Implementation
Code Walkthrough
Essential C# snippets you will use and test.
// Strategy interface
public interface IShippingStrategy
{
  double CalculateCost(Order order);
}

// USPS strategy
public class USPSStrategy : IShippingStrategy
{
  public double CalculateCost(Order order)
  {
    return 5.00 + (order.WeightInKg * 1.50);
  }
}

// FedEx strategy
public class FedExStrategy : IShippingStrategy
{
  public double CalculateCost(Order order)
  {
    return 8.00 + (order.VolumeInCubicMeters * 2.20);
  }
}
Testing tip
Create a sample Order and assert the cost returned by each strategy. This isolates algorithm logic from the context.
Null-safety
Check constructor and setter arguments in the context and throw ArgumentNullException if a null strategy is supplied.
Key Takeaway
Small, focused classes are easier to test and extend than a single monolithic conditional implementation.

screens.title: Strategy vs. Conditionals and Template Method
screens.narratorSegment: You must choose the right tool for the job. Strategy replaces complex conditionals with separate classes that implement a shared interface. This brings testability and easier extension: adding a strategy is adding a class rather than editing existing branches. However, if you only have one or two very stable algorithms with minimal logic, introducing multiple classes may add unnecessary complexity. That is the main reason to prefer simple conditionals in trivial cases. Template Method is an alternative when algorithms share a large amount of common structure but differ in a few steps. In Template Method you factor the common workflow into a base class and let subclasses override parts of it. In contrast, Strategy keeps each algorithm isolated and encourages composition over inheritance. A misunderstanding is thinking Strategy and Template Method are interchangeable; they address different trade-offs. Ask: do the algorithms share common steps or are they independent? If common, Template Method may be more concise; if independent, Strategy offers cleaner separation. Also consider testing effort — Strategy often simplifies testing each algorithm in isolation. Strategy vs. Conditionals and Template Method means use strategy for independent algorithms; choose template method when algorithms share a large common structure; use conditionals when logic is trivial and unlikely to change.. In practical terms, when to prefer strategy, when to stay simple, and when to use template method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Strategy vs Alternatives
Comparison: Conditionals, Strategy, Template Method
A quick decision guide to choose the right approach.
Conditionals
Best for trivial, stable choices. Low boilerplate but poor extensibility.
Strategy
Best when algorithms are independent, evolving, and need separate tests.
Template Method
Best when algorithms share a common skeleton but vary in specific steps.
Example — Use Strategy
Different shipping carriers with distinct formulas and independent logic.
Example — Use Template Method
Report generation where all reports follow a fixed pipeline but formatting steps differ.
Misconception
Strategy is not a panacea; pick the least complex pattern that satisfies maintainability and testing needs.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Refactor: Discount Calculator
Step-by-step Refactor
Follow these concrete steps to modernize the discount system.
1
Define IDiscountStrategy with ApplyDiscount(Order, double basePrice).
2
Implement NoDiscount, Seasonal, Loyalty, and FirstTime strategies using the previous switch logic.
3
Create NewDiscountCalculator that accepts an IDiscountStrategy and delegates ApplyDiscount.
4
Refactor Order to use strategy injection or let the client supply the strategy when calculating the final price.

Key Takeaway

Refactoring to Strategy isolates behavior and makes adding new discounts safe and testable without modifying the calculator core.

Starter code hint

Common Mistake
Do not let the NewDiscountCalculator create strategies from strings; inject them to keep the calculator decoupled.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Refactored Discount Strategy
Refactored Code Example
A compact Strategy-based replacement for the old switch-based calculator.
public interface IDiscountStrategy
{
  double ApplyDiscount(Order order, double basePrice);
}

public class SeasonalDiscountStrategy : IDiscountStrategy
{
  public double ApplyDiscount(Order order, double basePrice)
  {
    return basePrice * 0.90; // 10% off
  }
}

{

  {

    return basePrice;
  }
}

public class NewDiscountCalculator
{

  public NewDiscountCalculator(IDiscountStrategy strategy)
  {
    _strategy = strategy ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(strategy));
  }

  public double CalculateFinalPrice(Order order)
  {
    double basePrice = order.GetTotalPrice();
    return _strategy.ApplyDiscount(order, basePrice);
  }
}

screens.title: Swapping Strategies at Runtime
screens.narratorSegment: One of Strategy's most powerful features is runtime swapping: the ability to change the algorithm a context uses while the application runs. You implement this by providing a setter like SetStrategy or by passing a different strategy to a new context instance. In the shipping example, you can create a ShippingService with a USPS strategy, compute a cost, then call SetStrategy with a UPS strategy and compute a different cost for the same order. This makes it straightforward to support customer preferences, A/B testing, or switching algorithms based on runtime configuration. Test cases should include swapping strategies to validate the context delegates correctly. A pitfall is mutable shared state inside strategies. Prefer stateless strategy objects or document that strategies carry state and avoid sharing them across threads unless they are thread-safe. When using dependency injection frameworks, register strategies as transient if they are stateful; register them as singleton if they are stateless and safe to reuse. Always choose the lifetime that matches the strategy’s behavior to prevent subtle bugs. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Anti-patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Common mistakes often undermine Strategy’s benefits. The most frequent error is allowing the context to create or select concrete strategies by itself. When a context takes a string flag and constructs concrete classes, it becomes coupled to implementation details and loses testability. A better approach is to inject the strategy from the client or an IoC container. Another mistake is splitting behavior into too many trivial strategy classes that add noise with little benefit. Conversely, making strategies too broad defeats the purpose of encapsulation. Also watch for duplicated code across strategies; if you see a lot of repeated logic, factor the common parts into a helper or use an abstract base class. Finally, neglecting null-safety in the context constructor or setter leads to runtime failures. The example ApplicationLogger from the chapter shows why creating strategies inside the context is problematic. Instead, let the client or a composition root decide which strategy to provide so the context stays simple and test-friendly. Concrete examples and what they break.
• Context creates concrete strategies from strings — couples code and hinders testing.
• Excessive fragmentation — many tiny strategies increase maintenance overhead without benefit.

An ApplicationLogger that chooses and constructs loggers by string input makes it hard to test and violates dependency inversion.
Fix
Use constructor injection or a factory to supply strategies, keeping contexts decoupled and testable.

screens.title: Practical Use Cases for Strategy

screens.title: Design Trade-offs and Testing Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Applying Strategy introduces more classes, which is a deliberate trade-off for clarity and testability. More classes can increase perceived complexity, but they also localize changes. To manage this, keep each strategy focused on one algorithm and avoid leaking external concerns into strategy classes. For testing, write unit tests per strategy: create a representative Order, call the algorithm, and assert expected outputs. Integration tests should verify the context delegates to the strategy as expected, including when strategies are swapped at runtime. When strategies share code, extract common behavior into a helper or use a small abstract base class to reduce duplication. Also decide on lifetimes: stateless strategies are candidates for singleton reuse; stateful strategies should be transient or scoped in DI containers. Finally, document the expected responsibilities of a strategy so future contributors know whether state is allowed and how to register implementations. This reduces accidental misuse and maintains the pattern’s benefits in larger teams. Keep strategies cohesive and testable to realize benefits without raising maintenance costs.

Test strategies in isolation to catch algorithmic bugs early and keep contexts thin and stable.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why behavioral patterns matter and how the Strategy pattern helps you decouple algorithms from the clients that use them. Behavioral patterns focus on how objects interact and share responsibilities, which makes systems easier to change and test. The Strategy pattern is a classic example: it defines a common interface for related algorithms, implements each algorithm in a separate class, and lets the client pick or swap the algorithm at runtime. You will see a concrete C# example that models shipping cost calculations, and then a refactoring exercise that replaces a large switch statement with strategy classes. We will also examine common mistakes, such as coupling a context to concrete strategy creation, and practical guidance like when Strategy is overkill. By the end you should be able to choose, implement, and safely apply Strategy in small systems like discount calculators or larger subsystems like authentication. Consider where you have conditional logic tied to behavior; that is often where Strategy can reduce friction and increase testability.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and apply the Strategy pattern in real C# code. First, you will name the core purpose of behavioral patterns and explain how they distribute responsibility between objects. Second, you will recognize the problem Strategy solves — interchangeable algorithms — and contrast it with simpler conditionals. Third, you will implement Strategy in C# by defining an interface, creating concrete strategy classes, and injecting them into a context. Finally, you will spot scenarios where Strategy improves flexibility, such as shipping calculations, discount rules, validation, or export formats, and avoid common pitfalls like over-engineering or letting the context instantiate its strategies. Each objective maps to hands-on practice: reading code, writing small strategy implementations, and refactoring a switch-based discount calculator into a Strategy-based design. As you work, test each strategy independently so you build confidence and ensure design decisions reduce complexity rather than add it.

This second objectives slide emphasizes hands-on practice and common pitfalls to avoid. You will implement a Strategy-based design in C#, writing an interface and multiple concrete strategies, then inject them into a context class. As you code, you will write unit tests for each strategy so behavior is verified independently of the context. You will also learn to spot anti-patterns: when the context creates its own strategies, when strategies are too small or too large, and when a simple conditional is the clearer choice. The hands-on activity refactors a discount calculator with four discount types into a Strategy design. That task teaches the pattern end-to-end: design the interface, implement concrete strategies, wire a new context, and update the main method to show runtime swapping. Finally, you will learn to choose between Strategy and other patterns such as Template Method if strategies share a lot of common code. Practice and tests make the pattern safe to apply in real systems.

The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one in a separate class, and makes them interchangeable through a common interface. In plain terms, you move algorithm-specific code out of a client and into strategy classes that the client calls through an interface. A concrete example is shipping cost calculation: USPS, FedEx, and UPS each use distinct formulas. Instead of a large conditional inside ShippingCalculator, you create an IShippingStrategy interface and concrete strategies for each carrier. The context holds a reference to IShippingStrategy and delegates cost calculation to it. This removes conditional logic from the context and obeys the Open/Closed Principle — you can add a new carrier by adding a class rather than editing existing code. A common misconception is thinking Strategy always reduces complexity; if you have only a single simple algorithm that will not change, Strategy can be unnecessary boilerplate. The real benefit appears when algorithms vary, evolve, or must be tested independently. Try naming the responsibilities: the Strategy implements the algorithm, the Context delegates and remains ignorant of concrete types, and the Client composes them. How would you test one strategy in isolation? That question guides how you structure constructors and dependencies.

Understanding the roles in Strategy clarifies responsibilities and tests. The three key roles are Strategy, Concrete Strategy, and Context. The Strategy is an interface that declares the operation signature your algorithms share. Each Concrete Strategy implements that interface with a specific algorithm. The Context holds a reference to the Strategy interface and delegates the operation to the current strategy. In C#, you typically inject the strategy via the constructor or a setter so the context remains unaware of concrete types. For example, a ShippingService takes an IShippingStrategy in its constructor and calls CalculateCost on it. That service may expose a SetStrategy method to swap strategies at runtime. Tests should exercise each concrete strategy directly, asserting algorithmic results for representative orders. A common mistake is letting the context both decide and instantiate strategies; that couples the context to strategy implementations and prevents easy testing. If strategies share common helper code, factor it into a base class or shared utility instead of embedding it in each strategy. Now imagine adding tax calculations or promotional adjustments: those concerns might be separate strategies or combined carefully, depending on cohesion.

In C#, the interface might be IShippingStrategy with a CalculateCost method that accepts an Order. Each concrete strategy implements that method with carrier-specific logic. The sample code demonstrates USPS with a base rate plus weight, FedEx using volume, and UPS using a higher base rate plus a weight multiplier. Writing small, focused strategy classes helps you test each algorithm with representative orders. A practical test creates an Order with known values and asserts the returned cost. If different strategies share code, extract helpers into a utility or a base abstract class. Remember to guard against null strategies in the context by throwing an ArgumentNullException or by providing a default strategy to keep behavior explicit and safe. You must choose the right tool for the job. Strategy replaces complex conditionals with separate classes that implement a shared interface. This brings testability and easier extension: adding a strategy is adding a class rather than editing existing branches. In contrast, Strategy keeps each algorithm isolated and encourages composition over inheritance. Conversely, making strategies too broad defeats the purpose of encapsulation. Also watch for duplicated code across strategies; if you see a lot of repeated logic, factor the common parts into a helper or use an abstract base class. Finally, neglecting null-safety in the context constructor or setter leads to runtime failures. Strategy is widely applicable when different algorithms perform the same task. The chapter lists several practical examples: validation rules that vary by input type, file import/export formats like CSV or JSON, compression algorithms such as ZIP or GZIP, data persistence strategies for different database providers, and authentication methods like OAuth or JWT. Each of these cases benefits from encapsulating algorithmic differences behind an interface. For example, different authentication flows require distinct steps and credentials, which are cleanly isolated as strategies. Another advantage is being able to swap strategies for testing or to run A/B experiments. Applying Strategy introduces more classes, which is a deliberate trade-off for clarity and testability. More classes can increase perceived complexity, but they also localize changes. To manage this, keep each strategy focused on one algorithm and avoid leaking external concerns into strategy classes. For testing, write unit tests per strategy: create a representative Order, call the algorithm, and assert expected outputs. Integration tests should verify the context delegates to the strategy as expected, including when strategies are swapped at runtime. When strategies share code, extract common behavior into a helper or use a small abstract base class to reduce duplication. Also decide on lifetimes: stateless strategies are candidates for singleton reuse; stateful strategies should be transient or scoped in DI containers. Finally, document the expected responsibilities of a strategy so future contributors know whether state is allowed and how to register implementations.
